---
applyTo: "spec/**/*.rb"
---

# WebMock and VCR

- In request, feature, job and service specs, stub each HTTP request the code makes to another service, and assert that it was made. In those specs, you MUST NOT stub the service class that makes the request, e.g. `allow(NewsletterClient).to receive(:new)`. Action specs stub the service instead.
- In specs, stub requests with the service's helpers from `spec/support`, e.g. `stub_newsletter_create`. You MUST NOT call `stub_request` in a spec. When the helper you need doesn't exist yet, add it to the service's support file first.
- Put the stubs for each service in a helper module in `spec/support`, included in every spec, with one method for each response the specs need: success, error and timeout, e.g. `stub_newsletter_create`, `stub_newsletter_create_failure` and `stub_newsletter_create_timeout` in `NewsletterServiceHelpers` in `spec/support/newsletter_service.rb`. Start each name with `stub_`, then the service and the request, and return the WebMock stub.
- Inside a helper, stub an error with `.to_return(status: 500)` and a timeout with `.to_timeout`, e.g. `stub_request(:post, "https://newsletter.example.com/posts").to_timeout` in `stub_newsletter_create_timeout`.
- Call stub helpers inside the example. Avoid calling them in a `let` or `before` block. Keep the returned stub in a local variable and check it with `have_been_requested`, e.g. `newsletter_request = stub_newsletter_create` then `expect(newsletter_request).to have_been_requested`.
- When a spec checks what a request sent, add a matcher to the service's helper module, as a method that returns WebMock's `have_requested` matcher and passes its keywords to `with` only when there are any, because `with` raises an error when called with no options. Name it `have_requested_` followed by the same service and request as the stub, and use it on `WebMock`, e.g. `matcher = have_requested(:post, "https://newsletter.example.com/posts")` then `options.any? ? matcher.with(**options) : matcher` in `have_requested_newsletter_create(**options)`.
- Outside the service's own spec, check only the parts of the request the spec is about, with `hash_including`, e.g. `expect(WebMock).to have_requested_newsletter_create(body: hash_including(title: "Hello World"))`.
- When a service's SDK has its own stubs, use them instead of WebMock, e.g. `stub_responses` in the AWS SDK. When neither WebMock nor the SDK's stubs can reach the client, e.g. a socket client with no stubs such as the `mqtt` gem, use a fake client in `spec/support`, e.g. `FakeMqttClient`.
- Turn an SDK's stubs on for every spec in a `spec/support` file named after the SDK, and remove each service's stubbed responses after each spec, e.g. `Aws.config.update(stub_responses: true)` and `config.after { Aws.config.delete(:s3) }` in `spec/support/aws.rb`.
- Set a spec's AWS responses in `Aws.config` inside a helper in `spec/support`, e.g. `stub_post_backup_upload`, and check the request with a block that keeps its params, e.g. `Aws.config[:s3] = { stub_responses: { put_object: ->(context) { uploads << context.params; {} } } }` then `expect(uploads).to contain_exactly(hash_including(key: "posts/#{post.id}.json"))`.
- To test an AWS service failing, stub the response with the error's code, e.g. `Aws.config[:s3] = { stub_responses: { put_object: "ServiceUnavailable" } }`.
- Use a fake client only when neither WebMock nor the SDK's own stubs can reach the client. In request, feature, job and service specs, you MUST NOT stub the gem's client class or the service around it, e.g. `instance_double(MQTT::Client)` or `allow(PostNotifier).to receive(:default)`.
- Block the gem's real connections for every spec in a `before` hook in its support file, with a message that names the helpers to use, e.g. `config.before { allow(MQTT::Client).to receive(:connect).and_raise("Use stub_mqtt_connection or stub_mqtt_message") }` in `spec/support/mqtt.rb`, because `WebMock.disable_net_connect!` doesn't cover sockets.
- Define one fake in the gem's support file, named `Fake` then the client's class, e.g. `FakeMqttClient` in `spec/support/mqtt.rb`. Give it only the methods the app calls, with the real client's parameters. Record each outbound call, return queued inbound messages in order, and raise when the code reads a message that wasn't queued, so a spec never waits on a socket, e.g. `raise "No MQTT message queued. Add one with stub_mqtt_message" if queue.empty?` in `FakeMqttClient#get`.
- Give the fake its own spec outside `spec/support`, which checks that each public method, other than the readers for its recorded calls and queue, has the same parameters on the real client, e.g. `expect(described_class.instance_method(name).parameters).to eq(MQTT::Client.instance_method(name).parameters)` in `spec/fakes/fake_mqtt_client_spec.rb`.
- Return the fake from the gem's connect method, not from the service, so the service's own code runs, e.g. its pool, e.g. `allow(MQTT::Client).to receive(:connect).and_return(fake_mqtt_client)` in `stub_mqtt_connection`.
- Put the fake's stubs in a helper module in the gem's support file, with one `stub_` method for each inbound message or failure the specs need, named after the gem and the message, e.g. `stub_mqtt_message(topic, payload)`, `stub_mqtt_connection_failure` and `stub_mqtt_publish_failure` in `MqttHelpers`. Raise the gem's own error in failure helpers, e.g. `MQTT::Exception`. Queue one more message on each call to a message helper. You MUST NOT call `allow` on the fake in a spec. Add a helper instead.
- Check each outbound call with a `have_` matcher on the fake, named after the verb, the gem and the message, e.g. `have_published_mqtt_message`. Give it the call's arguments, with keywords for the parts to check, matched like `have_requested`. Parse a JSON payload inside the matcher, so specs check it with `hash_including`, e.g. `expect(fake_mqtt_client).to have_published_mqtt_message("posts/#{post.id}/published", payload: hash_including("title" => "Hello World"))`.
- Give each spec a new fake, and clear the service's cached connections after each spec, so no spec gets the last spec's client, e.g. `config.after { PostNotifier.const_get(:POOLS).clear }`.
- Test the service's connection code, e.g. reconnecting, keepalive and TLS, in one spec against a real broker or the gem's in-process server, e.g. `MQTT::FakeServer`. Use the fake client in every other spec. You MUST NOT test what the app does over a real socket.
